nameStory: This shiny beetle earned its 'June beetle' nickname because adults emerge in early summer, often appearing in large numbers during June. The 'green' part is obvious once you see one—their metallic emerald wings catch sunlight like tiny jewels buzzing through your garden.
description: The Common Green June Beetle is a chunky, metallic green beetle about the size of your thumbnail. Adults measure roughly 0.6 to 0.9 inches long, with dull green wing covers that shimmer in sunlight. Their sides flash golden, while their head, legs, and belly shine with brilliant metallic green that looks almost mirror-like.

idTips.label: Metallic green coloration
idTips.description: Body shimmers with dull metallic green on top, brilliant shiny green underneath—like a living emerald that catches and reflects light

idTips.label: Golden sides
idTips.description: Look for distinctive gold or bronze coloring along the edges where the wing covers meet the body

idTips.label: Daytime activity
idTips.description: Unlike many beetles that hide during day, these buzz around actively in bright sunlight, often crash-landing into windows or screens

idTips.label: Size and shape
idTips.description: Thumbnail-sized and chunky with a slightly flattened, oval shape—feels solid and heavy when it lands on you

idTips.label: Flight pattern
idTips.description: Flies with a distinctive loud buzzing sound, often appearing clumsy and crash-prone as they bumble from plant to plant

habitat: Found in gardens, orchards, and woodland edges where they feed on overripe fruit and tree sap. Adults prefer sunny areas with fruit trees, roses, and other flowering plants. They're most common in areas with sandy or well-drained soils where their grubs can develop underground.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging from soil in late spring, becoming more noticeable as temperatures warm. Look for early individuals on flowering trees and shrubs.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity from June through August when adults are most abundant and active during hot, sunny days. This is when you'll hear them buzzing around gardens and crashing into screens.
seasonality.fall: Adult activity decreases significantly by early fall. Grubs are developing underground, feeding on organic matter and plant roots.
seasonality.winter: Adults have died off and grubs overwinter deep in soil. No above-ground activity to observe during cold months.

funFact: These beetles are such poor fliers that they often crash-land upside down and can't flip themselves over—if you find one on its back buzzing helplessly, it's probably a Green June Beetle that needs a gentle nudge to get airborne again.
confusionNotes: Often confused with other June beetles, but most others are brown or reddish-brown rather than metallic green. Japanese beetles are smaller and have a more coppery-green color with white spots along their sides, while Green June Beetles are larger and uniformly metallic green.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'June beetles,' many people use 'June bug' to refer to any beetle that shows up around porch lights in summer. True Green June Beetles are actually day-active and aren't particularly attracted to lights, unlike their brown cousins that swarm around your evening barbecue.
compareHints: This is the only Cotinis species regularly found in New England, making identification easier than in southern states where multiple green scarab species overlap. Compared to other scarab beetles in the region, Green June Beetles are distinctly metallic green rather than brown, and they're active during daylight rather than being drawn to lights at night.
